sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) learns the state-action value function (Q-function) of target policy from an offline dataset collected by different behavior policy, which enables RL to reuse logged experience in real-world domains such as robotics (Levine et al., 2016; Kalashnikov et al., 2018) and industrial control (Zhan et al., 2022). However, off-policy value learning becomes harder as the effective horizon grows (Laidlaw et al., 2023), i.e., the number of transitions across which the critic must carry value information before reaching state whose value it already knows. Most off-policy actor-critic methods learn the critic with one-step temporal-difference (TD) backups (Fujimoto et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2020; Kostrikov et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023; Park et al., 2025c). one-step target bootstraps after single logged transition, which makes it robust to off-policy data but moves value back by only one transition per update. We show that the value error at state is exactly the sum of the one-step Bellman residuals along the rest of the trajectory, so critic can reach small TD loss and still misvalue the start states by an amount that grows with the horizon. Multi-step returns (Watkins, 1989; Sutton and Barto, 2018) or Q-chunking (Li et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2023) shorten this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps before bootstrapping. Nevertheless, this imposes trade-off between fast value propagation (longer backups) and low off-policy bias (shorter backups): we show that each spanned suboptimal action adds systematic bias that grows toward limit linear in H. Since offline trajectories could be mixed with suboptimal actions, no fixed backup length is optimal for every TD update. Per-decision off-policy corrections such as Retrace (Precup et al., 2000; Munos et al., 2016) make this choice at every transition with importance ratios. However, these ratios require policy densities, which flow or diffusion-based policies (Park et al., 2025c; Mao et al., 2024a; Li and Levine, 2026; Xu et al., 2026) do not expose. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), which shortens the effective horizon of Q-learning without inheriting the bias of suboptimal dataset actions. HQL achieves this by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns at every transition (Figure 1). More specifically, HQL attaches binary gate to every logged action, i.e., every action stored in the dataset: if the target critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, the gate is open and the 1 action π would keep suboptimal behavior action terminal (exact value) One-step TD each target reaches back one state Multi-step TD one long target, but it spans the suboptimal action HQL (ours) keep logged action only if gate is open gate open (c = 1): long trace gate cut (c = 0) suffix still learns Figure 1: Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL). Purple arcs show the reach of one training target. One-step TD accumulates residuals, and multi-step TD inherits the bias of the suboptimal action it spans (yellow). HQL compares each logged action with the best-of-N policy samples, continuing the trace where it passes (c=1) and cutting it where it fails (c=0, dashed), so reward travels far without inheriting off-policy bias. target continues through it for one more step; otherwise, the target falls back to one-step bootstrap. Our key observation is that this gate is principled without any density: for the optimal policy π µ exp(τ Q) that behavior-regularized RL approximates (Peters et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2025b), the behavior density cancels from the importance ratio, and as τ the largest gate that preserves Qπ becomes exactly the comparison of critic values. HQL uses an estimated behavior model only to sample action candidates and never evaluates its density. Since the gate depends only on the ordering of critic values, it is also invariant to the reward scale, and the only hyperparameter in HQL is the number of candidates . We evaluate HQL on combination-lock task, whose true Q-values are known exactly, and on longhorizon OGBench and OCBench tasks (Park et al., 2025a; Park and Levine, 2026). On the combination lock, HQL keeps the lowest value estimation error across different horizon, whereas one-step TD accumulates error and n-step TD fails on corrupted dataset. On OGBench and OCBench, at matched budget of critic targets, HQL outperforms one-step TD, n-step TD, Q-chunking (Li et al., 2025b), and Long-horizon Q-Learning (Abraham et al., 2026), especially on the most challenging long-horizon tasks. Perhaps surprisingly, we find that most of HQLs targets are one or few-step targets: HQL wins by choosing which targets to extend, not by extending them far.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Error propagation in value learning. Error propagation through bootstrapping has been studied for approximate value and policy iteration (Munos, 2005; Farahmand et al., 2010), TD with function approximation (Tsitsiklis and Roy, 1997), and n-step and TD(λ) updates (Kearns and Singh, 2000); its instability with off-policy data is the deadly triad (van Hasselt et al., 2018), and the horizon governs the difficulty of evaluation and learning (Liu et al., 2018; Laidlaw et al., 2023). Multi-step off-policy correction. Multi-step returns and eligibility traces shorten the backup chain (Watkins, 1989; Sutton and Barto, 2018; De Asis et al., 2018), and small fixed is standard in deep RL (Hessel et al., 2018; Kapturowski et al., 2019; Hernandez-Garcia and Sutton, 2019). Per-decision importance sampling (Precup et al., 2000) and its clipped variants (Retrace (Munos et al., 2016; Touati et al., 2018), off-policy Q(λ) (Harutyunyan et al., 2016), V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018), trajectory-aware traces (Daley et al., 2023)) correct the mismatch step by step, and emphatic TD reweights updates (Sutton et al., 2016). Watkinss Q(λ) cuts traces at non-greedy actions while Pengs Q(λ) keeps them (Peng and Williams, 1996; Kozuno et al., 2021; Kim and hwan Oh, 2026); other work adapts the trace (White and White, 2016; Rowland et al., 2020), avoids ratios via action-dependent bootstrapping (Mahmood et al., 2017), gates traces at non-greedy actions (Daley, 2026), or adds multi-step inequalities (Abraham et al., 2026). However, these corrections need action probabilities or discrete greedy target policy. 2 Horizon reduction. Instead of correcting within backup, horizon-reduction methods change what decision is. Hierarchical methods act over options or subgoals (Bacon et al., 2017; Vezhnevets et al., 2017; Nachum et al., 2018, 2019; Xu et al., 2022), and action chunking treats short action sequence as one decision (Seo and Abbeel, 2024; Li et al., 2025b,a; Song et al., 2026). However, within each segment they use fixed, uncorrected backup and inherit the bias; HQL is orthogonal and contains both as ungated special cases. Another line exploits the structure of goal-reaching tasks through quasimetric value functions (Wang et al., 2023a; Zheng et al., 2026), graph search over subgoals (Eysenbach et al., 2019), and goal-conditioned hierarchies (Park et al., 2023; Ahn et al., 2025; Zhou and Kao, 2025; Park et al., 2026). These methods rely on goal-reaching reward and thus apply only to goal-conditioned RL; in contrast, HQL makes no assumption on the reward. Policy extraction with expressive policies. Offline RL methods regularize the policy toward the data, either explicitly through divergence penalties (Wu et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021; Fujimoto and Gu, 2021) or implicitly through in-sample value learning and weighted behavior cloning (Peng et al., 2019; Nair et al., 2020; Kostrikov et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022, 2023, 2025a). Recent work extracts expressive diffusion or flow policies by value-guided training (Wang et al., 2023b; Mao et al., 2024a; Park et al., 2025c), rejection sampling from behavior model (Chen et al., 2023; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023), adjoint matching (Li and Levine, 2026), or value gradient flow (Xu et al., 2026). These methods keep one-step critic; HQL only changes the critics target and can serve any of them.

sections.title: 4 Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning
sections.content: In this section, we introduce Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL). We begin with gated multi-step target and design the gate based on value comparison (Section 4.1). We then show that this gate is limiting case of per-decision importance sampling yet needs no action density (Section 4.2). Finally, we provide several practical considerations for HQL and discuss its connection to previous work (Section 4.3). 4.1 Gated Multi-Step Targets Our key idea is to let backup continue through logged action only when that action is at least as good as the actions the target policy would take, i.e., its advantage under the target policy is non-negative, which keeps it out of the bias term of Eq. 3 while reducing the horizon of TD learning via multi-step bootstrapping. To do so, we attach gate ci {0, 1} to every transition and define the HQL target backward along logged segment, hql = rt + γ {z one-step target (st+1) } π + γ ct+1 (cid:0)Y hql t+1 Q(st+1, at+1)(cid:1) } {z downstream correction , (6) with the correction set to zero at the end of the segment, and γ kept for generality. Intuitively, the first term is the usual one-step bootstrap from the target policy, and the second term carries back whatever the logged continuation has learned beyond the critics current estimate at (st+1, at+1). When the gate accepts at+1, this correction flows back and the target extends one more step; when it rejects at+1, the target is plain one-step target, and the states after the cut still start their own targets (as shown in Figure 1, bottom). Unrolling the recursion, run of accepted actions yields multi-step target whose length is set by the data rather than fixed in advance. Note that 0 recovers one-step TD and 1 is the uncorrected multi-step return. It remains to decide when the gate is open, i.e., whether the target policy would keep the logged action. Intuitively, logged action is safe to follow if it is at least as good as what the policy itself would propose, which the critic can check by comparing the logged action with candidates drawn from the policys own sampler: (cid:20) ci = Q(si, ai) max 1mN (cid:21) Q(cid:0)si, a(m) (cid:1) , a(m) µ(si), (7) where µ is the behavior policy that can be estimated using any advanced generative models from D. In other words, the logged action is kept if it is at least as good as the best of policy proposals. Note that the gate depends only on an ordering of critic values, so it is invariant to the scale of Q, needs no behavior density, and has as its only hyperparameter; it costs behavior samples and critic evaluations per transition, the same as the best-of-N bootstrap already requires. 4 Algorithm 1 Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (critic update) Require: dataset D, window length H, gate width , target budget 1: Sample B/H windows (st, at, rt, . . . , st+H ) of consecutive transitions from 2: At every position i: draw a(1:N ) 3: For = 1, . . . , 0: compute hql 4: Regress all pairs (st+j, at+j) onto sg(Y hql µ(si) and compute the gate ci (Eq. 7) t+j by Eq. 6, with no correction at = 1 t+j ); update i

sections.title: 4.2 A Density-Free Gate via Per-Decision Importance Sampling
sections.content: A remaining question is whether cutting multi-step backups with this gate is principled, since cutting changes what multi-step backup converges to. Per-decision importance sampling answers this (Precup et al., 2000; Munos et al., 2016): in the tabular setting, any gate ci [0, 1] with ci π(aisi)/µ(aisi) preserves Qπ as the fixed point of Eq. 6, and we call such gate valid. However, evaluating this bound requires the density ratio π/µ, which is unavailable and hard to estimate (Mao et al., 2024b; Xu et al., 2025a) when using generative policies, or when policies are implicit, e.g., µ is flow sampler and π selects among its samples. Fortunately, the ratio has closed form for the policy that behavior-regularized RL methods approximate, i.e., the exponential tilt of the behavior policy (Peters et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2023; Li and Levine, 2026), πθ(as) = µ(as) exp(τ Q(s, a)) Z(s) , Z(s) = Eaµ(s) [exp(τ Q(s, a))] , (8) so the behavior density cancels and log(π/µ)(aisi) = τ Q(si, ai) log Z(si). We estimate the normalizer from behavior samples as (cid:91)log Z(si) = LSEm(τ Q(si, a(m) )) log , where LSEm(xm) = log PN m=1 exp(xm) is the log-sum-exp, and clipping the ratio at one gives the largest valid gate ci = exp (cid:16) min 0, τ Q(si, ai) (cid:91)log Z(si) o(cid:17) . (9) This soft gate interpolates between two extremes. As τ 0, every gate equals one and the target is an uncorrected multi-step return. As τ , the tilt concentrates on the best behavior-supported action, and because LSEm(xm) maxm xm + log , the exponent is nonnegative at any τ when no candidate beats the logged action and tends to otherwise, so the soft gate becomes exactly the value comparison of Eq. 7. Therefore, HQLs gate is the τ limit of valid gate, which is more scalable and robust since it avoids temperature and can be computed without density. It also outperforms the soft gate at every τ we tried (Appendix A.7). 4.3 Practical Considerations Dense targets over trajectory window. Since HQL is not restricted to fixed n-step backup, it does not need to compute target only at the first state of sampled segment. Instead, HQL samples trajectory window (st, at, rt, . . . , st+H ) of consecutive transitions and computes the gated multi-step target for every stateaction pair in the window. More specifically, it computes the gates ci once at every position, evaluates Eq. 6 backward from the window end, and regresses each (st+j, at+j) onto its own target hql t+j , = 0, . . . , 1, masking positions beyond an episode boundary (Algorithm 1). By doing so, window yields targets whose maximal reach decreases from to 1, and the gate can shorten each of them further. To enable fair comparison, we hold the number of critic targets per update fixed: with budget of B, one-step TD samples transitions and HQL samples B/H windows. L=1, H=4: HQL gate open for 3 decisions, then cut L=2, H=1: Q-chunking one chunk, nothing to gate L=2, H=4: Chunked-HQL at stride 3 decisions = 6 steps kept, then cut Figure 2: HQL and Chunked-HQL. sets how many decisions one target chains, and how many environment steps each decision covers. 5 Multi-step decisions via Chunked-HQL. So far the decision stride is fixed to 1, meaning each decision corresponds to single environment step. To allow for more flexible decision-making, we let one decision span several environment steps. More specifically, with stride L, decision is chunk of primitive actions that the critic scores as unit, Q(st, at:t+L), and window of chunks reaches LH environment steps while still producing targets. Note that the gate is unchanged, now comparing the logged chunk with the best-of-N chunks drawn from the policy, and the backup of Eq. 6 holds with γL in place of γ and per-chunk reward sums. Connections to existing methods. To summarize, in HQL or Chunked-HQL, sets how many environment steps one decision covers, and sets how many decisions one target may chain (Figure 2). With L=1, H=1 gives one-step TD, an ungated window of size gives uncorrected H-step TD, and gated window gives HQL. With L=k, H=1 is Q-chunking with chunks of actions (Li et al., 2025b), since single chunk leaves nothing to gate, and H>1 gives Chunked-HQL at stride k. Note that the two variables extend the maximal reach of target, environment steps, in different ways. Increasing lets one target makes more decisions while the policy outputs less actions per step, and the gate decides for each target how many of these decisions it actually uses. In contrast, increasing makes each decision cover more environment steps, but each chunk then runs open loop and the policy must search larger, dim(A)-dimensional action space.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: The goal of our experiments is to answer four questions. (Q1) Does HQL enable better value learning under different horizon lengths and dataset suboptimality? (Q2) How does HQL compare with TD and other baselines on OGBench and OCBench? (Q3) Does HQL work with different policy-extraction methods? (Q4) How do the different components of HQL affect its performance? 5.1 Experimental Setup Combination lock. For Q1, we use modified combination-lock chain (Park et al., 2025b) with linearly ordered states and two actions: the correct one advances to the next state and the other returns to the first state, with reward -1 per step and 0 at the terminal state. The offline dataset consists of length-n=64 windows (64 transitions each): for every stateaction pair we roll out M=100 windows that start with that pair and then follow the correct action, truncating window early if it reaches the terminal state. Following Park et al. (2025b), we construct datasets of n-step trajectory windows with uniform coverage of starting state-action pairs. To study the effect of increasing action corruption, we independently replace each of the 1 = 63 subsequent actions with the non-optimal action with probability {0, 0.002, 0.005, 0.011, 0.022}, chosen so that in expectation (1p)63 {100, 88, 73, 50, 25}% of windows are clean, i.e. contain no corrupted action. We use {512, 1024, 2048, 4096}, giving 2HM windows per dataset. Because the dynamics are deterministic, the ground-truth is available in closed form (A.3). OGBench. Q2Q4 use six state-based OGBench configurations (Park et al., 2025a): cube-double, cube-triple, scene (sparse reward), humanoidmaze-medium, antmaze-giant and humanoidmaze-giant, whose task horizons last 500 to 4000 steps  (Table 5)  ; we report the mean score over each configurations five tasks. Runs train for 1M offline and then 1M online steps, with 50 evaluation episodes every 105 steps; runs score is the mean of its last three evaluations. OCBench. To test HQL on even longer horizons, we also use OCBench (Park and Levine, 2026), robotic manipulation benchmark whose datasets come from scripted policies with properties similar to human demonstrations. We take eight full-frequency (50 Hz) tasks from four domains (block, chamber, switch, hanoi), whose episodes last 1000 to 5000 steps. Following the RL baselines of OCBench, all methods use 25-step action chunks, 8 2048 residual MLPs, an HL-Gauss critic and γ=0.9999, with 1024 critic targets per update. Runs train for 1M offline and 1.5M online steps with 500 evaluation episodes every 5 104 steps (Appendix A.6). Baselines. We compare HQL (H = 16) with existing baselines under matched compute budget: every method receives 512 critic targets per gradient step. We consider three TD baselines. 16-window TD uses the same windows and batch as HQL but removes the gate, so comparing the two isolates the gates effect. 8-step TD (n=8 matches the average reach of 16-step window) and 1-step TD each regress single target per sequence with batch of 512. We also compare with Q-chunking (QC) (Li et al., 2025b), which treats chunk of 8 actions as single decision and bears no off-policy bias, and Long-horizon Q-Learning (LQL) (Abraham et al., 2026), which adds hinge penalties to one-step TD that enforce 6 Figure 3: Combination lock. HQL remains accurate under data corruption as the horizon grows. The figure illustrates the RMSE between the learned Qθ and the true Q, averaged uniformly over all 2H stateaction pairs of the corrupted combination lock, after 1M updates (log scale). Panels vary the corruption fraction of the dataset. n-step TD (n = 64) diverges as soon as any corruption is present; 1-step TD is unaffected by corruption but its error grows sharply with the horizon H. multi-step inequalities along the logged trajectory. All methods share the same critic architecture and use the same behavior flow policy with best-of-N sampling. 5.2 Q1: Toy Example with Corrupted Windows Figure 3 supports both halves of the analysis. On clean data, the error of 1-step TD grows by three orders of magnitude from H=512 to 4096, while 64-step TD and HQL avoid this accumulation. As the corruption rate increases, 64-step TD degrades sharply, because each target sums the negative advantages of the actions it spans. HQL cuts the trace at those actions: its error stays below both 1-step TD and 64-step TD at every horizon. 5.3 Q2: Results on OGBench and OCBench HQL is the strongest method across all six domains. HQL reaches mean success rate of 0.74 against 0.49 for the best TD baseline, 8-step TD (Figure 4). Consistent with our analysis in Section 3.1, the gap is largest on the four configurations with the largest horizons of 1000 steps or more  (Table 5)  ; on cube-triple, HQL reaches 0.54 while both multi-step baselines score 0. 16-window TD matches HQL in everything except the gate, yet it is the weakest method on average, this demonstrates the effectiveness of gating in HQL. Comparison with other baselines. At the same budget and sampling width  (Table 1)  , HQL improves the mean success rate by 12% over LQL and by 29% over QC. QC is best on cube-double and scene but scores 0% on both humanoid mazes. Table 1: HQL and Chunked-HQL against LQL and QC. Success rates (%) are averaged over five tasks and reported as offline online with standard error over five seeds; we bold the best offline and the best online score at integer level. HQL and Chunked-HQL achieve the best results, especially on the long-horizon tasks. Although Q-chunking avoids the offpolicy bias by having the critic to score the whole L-sized action chunk Q(st, at:t+L), it falls short because the critic must choose among dim(A)-dimensional chunks, and fixed best-of-N search covers that space increasingly sparsely as the chunk size grows. Second, each chunk runs open loop for L-steps (we choose = 8 while running QC), so the agent cannot correct its action within chunk. This also explains why QC performs well on cube-double and scene, whose chunks are low-dimensional (please refer to table 5 for action dimensions of the different OGBench tasks), but trails on antmaze-giant and fails on both humanoid mazes. We expect wider best-of-N search to help QC, since it covers the chunk space more densely, though at cost in samples and critic evaluations that grows with . Success rate on eight 50 Hz tasks (one seed, smoothed over three evaluations; numbers are the mean of the last three). All methods use 25-step chunks and the same best-of-16 bootstrap. Chunked-HQL matches or outperforms both baselines on all eight tasks, especially on switch and chamber-medium. Why does HQL help? One might expect multi-step method to win by sending reward information far back along the trajectory. To understand why HQL works better than the TD baselines, we log how many steps each targets trace survives (Figure 6). Perhaps surprisingly, the actual traces are short: 77% of targets are exactly one-step targets while 17% extend to two steps and 6% to three or more steps, and none exceeds six of the sixteen available steps. This indicates that HQL helps not by making targets longer but by choosing which ones to extend: n-step TD extends all of them and inherits the bias of every action spanned, 1-step TD extends none, and HQL extends target only when its logged action passes the gate. 8 Figure 6: Per-target trace length with the memoryless prediction (dashed). On OCBench, we compare ChunkedHQL (L=25, H=8, i.e., 200-step window) with n-step TD at {100, 200}, which regresses the chunk critic onto an uncorrected n-step return and is the backup used by OCBenchs own RL baselines (n=200). Motivated by Section 5.5, we decouple the two widths of HQL: the gate uses =2, while the bootstrap and acting use best-of-16 as in the baselines. Chunked-HQL reaches mean success rate of 0.82 at 2.5M steps against 0.53 for 100-step TD and 0.46 for 200-step TD (Figure 5). The gap is largest on switch-3x3 (0.91 vs. 0.15), switch-4x4 (0.76 vs. 0.17) and chamber-medium (0.53 vs. 0.12), where the n-step baselines barely improve or even degrade during online training. Note that 200-step TD is worse than 100-step TD on seven of the eight tasks, which agrees with Eq. 3: longer uncorrected return sums the negative advantages of more logged actions, while the gate lets HQL extend target only through chunks that pass the value comparison. 5.4 Q3: Combining HQL with Other Policy Extraction Methods HQL with QAM. Q-learning with adjoint matching (QAM) (Li and Levine, 2026) trains flow policy to sample from the tilted distribution π µ exp(τ Q). sections.title: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.content: In this paper, we propose HQL, which shortens the effective horizon of Q-learning without inheriting the bias of suboptimal logged actions. HQL gates each logged action with density-free value comparison and achieves strong results on long-horizon OGBench tasks, both alone and as drop-in critic for QAM and VGF. We believe that HQL represents concrete step toward horizon-scalable off-policy RL. One limitation is that the gate relies on the critics own ranking. One future work is to apply HQL over subgoals in hierarchical manner.

All runs use H=8, batch of 128 windows (1024 critic targets per update), 1M offline and 1M online steps, and one seed; the soft gate estimates log ˆZ and acts with 16 behavior samples, and the hard gate uses =4 for both. Figure 10 and Table 7 show that the hard gate achieves the best mean success rate (61%), and that the soft gate improves steadily as τ increases (36% 57%), i.e., as it approaches the hard gate. The gap is largest on the long-horizon mazes: on humanoidmaze-medium the hard gate reaches 91% against 77% for the best soft gate, and on antmaze-giant 65% against 58%. The soft gate is only better on cube-double at τ =1, while scene and puzzle-3x3 end at the same value for every gate. This indicates that the hard gate is not only the limit that removes τ as hyperparameter, but also the strongest member of the family: finite τ keeps partial credit for suboptimal logged actions, so the multi-step target inherits part of their bias, which is exactly the failure mode of uncorrected n-step TD. 18 Table 6: Hyperparameters for the OCBench benchmark experiment (Figure 5).
